However, we would like to clarify that the time-reversal- symmetry-breaking spin-singlet superconducting states cannot explain the observed re- entrance in superconductivity under an applied magnetic field. Excluding the possibility for spin-singlet superconducting states: After meticulously ruling out trivial origins, especially the vortex physics, the reentrance in superconducting states cannot be explained by time-reversal symmetry breaking spin-singlet pairing. The reason is that the Zeeman effect of the magnetic field tends to suppress the spin-singlet superconducting state by inducing a depairing effect on spin-singlet Cooper pairs, whereas it does not affect the equal-spin pairing states. Therefore, the reappearance of the superconducting state under a larger magnetic field is not consistent with the spin-singlet Cooper pairs scenario. Instead, the observed re-entrance is more consistent with equal-spin pairing, where the spin magnetic moments of the Cooper pairs couple to the magnetic field, lowering the energy of the superconducting state. To clarify this point, we have revised the main text as follows: “In addition to the pronounced hysteresis, the observation of re-entrant superconductivity as the magnetic field increases suggests that the SC-II phase can be stabilized by the magnetic field. After carefully ruling out trivial origins, the spin- singlet scenario cannot support the field-induced re-entrant superconductivity. This is because the Zeeman effect of the magnetic field tends to suppress the spin-singlet superconducting state by inducing a depairing effect on spin-singlet Cooper pairs, whereas it does not affect the equal-spin pairing states. Therefore, the reappearance of the superconducting state under a larger magnetic field is not consistent to the spin-singlet Cooper pairs scenario. Instead, the observed re-entrance is more consistent with equal-spin pairing, where the spin-magnetic moments of the Cooper pairs couple to the magnetic field, lowering the energy of the superconducting state.” Comments 3: In the explanation of their proposed mechanism, the authors do not address the effect of out-of-plane magnetic fields as seen in their measurements. In the model involving superconducting domains, why should an out-of-plane field component destroy hysteresis? Response: We thank the referee for this very insightful question. As noted in Chinese Phys. Lett. 38, 037403 (2021), RbV₃Sb₅ is a quasi-two-dimensional superconductor, where the out-of-plane resistivity is approximately 33 times greater than the in-plane resistivity at low temperatures. In such materials, an out-of-plane magnetic field rapidly suppresses superconductivity due to the orbital effects, which generates many vortices within the superconducting plane. When the applied magnetic field has a sizable out-of-plane component, many vortices will be created, and the vortices will dominate the transport properties of the superconducting films. As the transport is primarily dominated by vortices, the magnetoresistance behaves in a similar way for both the up-sweep and down-sweep fields. Therefore, the magnetoresistance hysteresis is weakened by the out-of-plane component of the magnetic field. As shown in Fig. R11 (Fig. 2g in the main text), the upper critical field decreases rapidly as the out-of-plane tilt angle of the magnetic field increases, which is consistent with our expectation above. Fig.R11. The out-of-plane angle dependence of the magnetoresistance, adapted from Fig. 2g in the manuscript. To address this point, we have revised the main text as follows: “ Moreover, as shown in Fig. 2g, the magnetoresistance hysteresis is weakened by the out-of-plane component of the magnetic field. The reason is as follows: RbV₃Sb₅ is a quasi-two-dimensional superconductor75, where the out-of-plane resistivity is approximately 33 times greater than the in-plane resistivity at low temperatures. In such materials, an out-of-plane magnetic field rapidly suppresses superconductivity due to the orbital effects, which generates many vortices within the superconducting plane. When the applied magnetic field has a sizable out-of-plane component, many vortices will be created, and the vortices will dominate the transport properties of the superconducting films. As the transport is mostly dominated by vortices, the magnetoresistance behaves in a similar way for both the up-sweep and down-sweep fields, leading to the disappearance of hysteresis. A similar behavior is also observed in the heavy-fermion superconductor UCoGe76, where a slight tilt of the magnetic field toward the c-axis leads to a significant decrease in the upper critical field and the disappearance of hysteresis.” Comments 4: It would be useful to see data showing if there are any memory effects. For example, if the sample goes from -1 T to 1 T, back to -1 T and again to 1 T, does the initial forwards sweep look the same as the second forward sweep? Fig. R12. The magnetoresistance curves show no memory effects since three consecutive magnetic field sweeps exhibit no discernible differences. Response: We thank the referee for this helpful comment. As demonstrated in Fig. R12, no memory effects are observed during three consecutive sweeps of the magnetic field between±1 T. This lack of memory effect suggests its intrinsic reversibility under magnetic fields, driven by spin-triplet pairing. We have added this result to our new Supplementary Information (Fig. S11). Comments 5: Given the difference in critical fields for different field directions, it is interesting to note that the split between SC-I and SC-II seems to occur at the same 0.2 Ω 3 2 1 r n s d d t magnetic field value regardless of the magnetic field direction, if I am interpreting Fig. S6 correctly. I am curious if the authors have any comment on this behavior. Response: We thank the referee for this very insightful question. The upper critical field of our sample shows a clear two-fold symmetry, as shown in Fig. R13. This two-fold symmetry provides evidence that there is nematicity in the normal state. For a sample with finite thickness, the nematicity effect dominates the upper critical field and gives rise to the two-fold symmetry. However, the magnetic field-driven re-entrance is due to the Zeeman coupling between the magnetic field and the spin-magnetic moments of the Cooper pairs, which is nearly independent of the magnetic field direction. Therefore, we expect that the critical magnetic field of the reentrance, which is controlled by the Zeeman effect, is insensitive to the magnetic field direction. Fig.R13. The re-entrant superconductivity under different in-plane magnetic fields with angles ranging from -180° to 180°. Comments 6: The similarity between the hysteresis seen in this compound and that observed in UCoGe is interesting; see Appl. Phys. Lett. 98, 132507 (2011). The hysteresis in UCoGe has the same qualitative behavior and also disappears for fields tilted slightly out of plane. I believe this similarity merits at least a mention, if not discussion. Response: We thank the referee for providing this useful information. We agree that this interesting work should be mentioned. The in-plane hysteresis observed in our work is indeed similar to the behavior seen in heavy fermion superconductors UCoGe. In both cases, a slight tilt of the magnetic field toward the c-axis leads to a significant decrease in the upper critical field and the disappearance of hysteresis. We have incorporated the relevant citation into the manuscript to highlight this connection: “A similar behavior is also observed in the heavy-fermion superconductor UCoGe76, where a slight tilt of the magnetic field toward the c-axis leads to a significant decrease in the upper critical field and the disappearance of hysteresis.” In addition, certain points in the text could benefit from clarification: •In the abstract: “Strikingly, at a fixed magnetic field, the finite-resistance state can be quenched to the zero-resistance state by applying a large current.” If I understand correctly, the statement should be: “…by applying and subsequently removing a large current.” It also might be worth noting here that the purpose of the current is sample heating. •Lines 13-15: “In addition, at a fixed magnetic field, a large current can suppress superconductivity completely at the finite-resistance state by heating. Incredibly, upon the removal of the current and cooling, the sample can be quenched to a zero-resistance state.” I understand why the authors refer to superconductivity in the finite-resistance state, having read the full article. For the sake of introducing the subject to new readers, I suggest something like the following: “In addition, by heating the sample with a large current and subsequently cooling it, all at a fixed magnetic field within the hysteresis loop, the sample can be brought from a finite-resistance state to a zero-resistance state.” •Lines 35-36: “Each V-Sb slab exhibits a two-dimensional (2D) kagome net of V atoms, forming a hexagonal structure with Sb atoms occupying central positions…” I believe it would be more accurate to say, “Each V-Sb slab exhibits a two-dimensional (2D) kagome net of V atoms, with Sb atoms occupying central positions of the hexagons within the kagome lattice…” Response: We are deeply grateful for the referee’s exceptionally thorough and thoughtful review. We fully agree with your suggestions and have carefully incorporated the advice into the revised manuscript. Comments: Throughout the text, “quench” is used to refer to the heating of the sample above the superconducting temperature as well as the cooling of the sample. This terminology is somewhat confusing, as “quench” can be used to refer to superconducting magnets unintentionally becoming normal, or to a quick-cooling process. It may be more clear to refer simply to heating and cooling via current. Response: We thank the referee for this very helpful suggestion. We agree that the terminology “quench” may lead to confusion, so we replaced it with “current heating and cooling,” as you suggested. Comments: Were all sweeps starting at a finite magnetic field actually cooled in that field, as opposed to zero-field-cooled? If so, was in-field cooling always done from room temperature, or from some other temperature? Response: To clarify, the measurement process begins with the sample being cooled in zero field, after which the magnetic field is swept. During the initial sweep from 0 to 1 T, the superconducting domains are aligned. Then, the subsequent sweeps (1 T to -1 T and -1 T to 1 T) are performed, as shown in our earlier response regarding the absence of memory effects. Additionally, we performed a field-cooling process, where the sample was cooled under a 1 T field and then sweeping the magnetic field from 1 T to -1 T and -1 T to 1 T. The results from the field-cooling process and zero-field-cooling process (sweeping between ±1 T after zero-field cooling) are identical. Comments: In the section “A proposed mechanism…”, when discussing the current heating/cooling experiment, the authors could be more explicit that in their model, cooling under an applied field results in superconducting domains that are predominantly aligned with the field, thus leading to a zero-resistance state. Response: We thank the referee for this suggestion. We modified the text as: “Moreover, at a fixed positive magnetic field ~ 0.27 T (Fig. 2h), we can use a large current to heat the metastable finite-resistance state with both positive and negative domains and then remove the current under a fixed magnetic field, the system can transition to the superconducting ground state, where superconducting domains predominantly align with the applied magnetic field. This current heating and cooling experiment strongly supports the superconducting domain picture of our theory which suggests that the SC-II state is a metastable state containing superconducting domains with different spin polarizations.” Comments: In Fig. S3a, “lower critical field” is used. I believe the authors are referring to the critical field that is at a lower value due to hysteresis. However, given that “lower critical field” already has a defined meaning for superconductors, a different term should be used (perhaps “greater” and “lesser” critical fields?) and the caption should clarify what is meant by these. Response: We thank the referee for this excellent suggestion. To avoid any potential ambiguity or misunderstanding, we have revised the text to use the terms ‘greater’ and ‘lesser’ instead. Comments: The caption of Fig. S6 indicates that it is showing data for a variety of magnetic field directions, presumably with the current direction fixed. However, the text (lines 166-168) says, “In RbV Sb , the re-entrant superconductivity appears in all 3 5 current directions with respect to a fixed in-plane magnetic field direction (as shown in Fig. S6 of Supplementary Information).” Which of these is accurate? Response: We apologize for the earlier misinformation and appreciate your attention to this detail. To clarify, we used a 3D vector magnet to rotate the in-plane magnetic field while keeping the current direction fixed. We have now corrected this in the manuscript. Comments: Additionally, at what temperature were the data for Fig. S6 taken? This should be indicated in the figure caption. •Similarly, at what temperature were the data for Fig. 3c taken? This should be indicated in the figure caption. Response: We thank the referee for these comments. The temperature information has been modified. Comments: Is the normal-state resistance of the sample actually 1 Ohm, as shown in Fig. 1d, or is this a normalization? Response: Yes, the actual measured resistance of the sample is around 1 Ohm, not a normalization. Comments: The authors cite Ref. 22 on line 143 when discussing the superheating- supercooling effect. However, I do not believe that Ref. 22 touches on superheating/supercooling. Is this the correct reference? The following changes are also suggested to improve figure legibility: •Adding tick marks along the axes for all figures that don’t have them: 2d, 3a, 3c, S4, S5a&b, S6a Response: We thank the referee for these comments. The citation has been modified, and the tick marks have been added. Comments: Possibly adding arrows and/or labels to Fig. 2h along the “quenching” segments, to indicate the heating and subsequent cooling •Changing the color of font used for “T1” and “T2” in Fig. 4 to make them more visible against the background color Response: We added arrows in Fig. 2h and changed the color of font to white. Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author): I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 1

First I'd like to thank the authors for putting together such a detailed response, including further measurements. I appreciate that this takes a lot of time and effort.
Unfortunately, I do not think that the case for p-wave superconductivity has been strengthened. While I appreciate that the authors have added "Signatures of" to the title, I don't think this qualifier is sufficient. I think claims of p-wave need to be robust, and I do not see robust evidence here.
1) Regarding hysteresis. The authors claim to have measured 10 CsV3Sb5 samples and seen no hysteresis. They show data for only one sample, however, and this sample DOES show hysteresis. This is seen as a shift in the "forward sweeping" curve compared to the "backward sweeping" curve. This is particularly clear in the vector version of the image show in the SI (as opposed to the bitmap in the rebuttal), where one can zoom in. The hysteresis is approximately 40 mT. This is not particularly different than the hysteresis the authors see for RbV3Sb5, which is around 250 mT at most. Crucially, the size of the hysteresis depends sensitively on angle, and without an angle dependence for the CsV3Sb5 sample, it is unclear that the authors are actually at 0 degrees (if they were off by even 5 degrees then they would see a substantial reduction in hysteresis, as per figure 2 in the main text). While the hysteresis seen in the CsV3Sb5 sample is fractionally smaller than the value of Bc itself, I have no reason to believe that it SHOULD be scaling with Bc.
It is worth noting that there is now another paper on the arxiv https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.13164v1 that sees hysteresis in CsV3Sb5 devices and claims that this supports chiral superconductivity in THAT material as well. I do not find their claims to be convincing, either.
2) Regarding arguments about resistance minima in the hysteresis curves: the theory that the authors cite, as well as the two measurements they show, are for granular superconductors. It is clear that granular superconductors will behave differently in a magnetic field than single crystals do because the nature of the pinning sites is completely different. I don't think this comparison is valid for the present study, which uses single crystals.
3) Regarding "nematicity". The authors state in their rebuttal that "Therefore, we fully agree with the referee that the symmetry breaking from D6h to D2h is a result of the normal-state nematicity. The superconducting state itself is not a reason for the symmetry breaking." If that is the case, then I do not understand why the authors are including the anisotropy in upper critical field at all. In the SI, they use a triplet state to explain the anisotropy in the upper critical field, and make connections to calculations that show "The upper critical field exhibit anisotropic behavior in single-layer limit when considering both the spin orbital-parity-coupling effect and nematic normal state."
I don't understand why "spin orbital parity coupling" is needed at all, in fact. Once the symmetry is D2h, an "s-wave" superconductor, with exactly zero spin orbit coupling, can have an anisotropic Hc2. For example, both the phonons and the density of states will have D2h symmetry, so there is no reason that the critical field should not as well. So I don't understand this argument about a "spin orbital-parity-coupling effect".
4) Regarding reentrance and zero resistance: the authors essentially attribute the lack of zero resistance and the lack of reproducibility on the reentrant behaviour to device inhomogeneity, invoking percolation and disorder even at temperatures as low as 100 mK, allegedly. It is extremely hard to understand how one could rule out flux trapping as a source of hysteresis if the devices are this inhomogeneous. This also directly contradicts the earlier statement "If the observed hysteresis were due to trivial mechanisms, such as flux trapping, rather than intrinsic properties of the superconducting states, it should also appear in CsV₃Sb₅ as well." If it is indeed an intrinsic property of the superconducting state, then why does it only occur in ~50% of the samples studied?
Even more concerning, in response to point 4 (the Pauli limit), the authors write "In the main text, we presented the data for Sample 1 (Fig. 2b) which has a thickness of (cid:1)0 = 27.6 nm. Given the layer separation of about 1 nm, our sample is far from the atomically thin limit." This directly contradicts what the authors wrote in response to point 3, "Unlike bulk superconductors, thin films are quasi-2D systems that are particularly susceptible to quasiparticles, thermal fluctuations, and fabrication defects". 27.6 nm is not anywhere near the "thin film" limit where thermal fluctuations could play such a role.
5) Regarding orbital suppression. If the resistivity ratio is approximately 33, then, if the critical field is orbital limited, the ratio of Hc2_ab to Hc2_c should be equal to (rho_c/rho_ab)^.5 = 6 (see e.g. https://journals.aps.org/rmp/abstract/10.1103/RevModPhys.66.1125) While I cannot find data on these devices for B||c, studies I can find (e.g. https://journals.aps.org/prresearch/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevResearch.3.043018) suggest that the ratio of Hc2_ab to Hc2_c is only half this value (i.e. it is more strongly suppressed for field in plane than if it was orbitally limited based on the resistance ratio). This suggests it is instead pauli limited for field in plane.

### Reviewer 2

The authors have properly addressed most of my questions, and the manuscript has been improved after the revision.
However, I still have a few minor suggestions and comments. Once there are addressed, the paper should be suitable for publication in Nature communications. My comments are as follows:
1. It seems that pairing states of CsV3Sb5 and RbV3Sb5 are different, at least according to experimental evidence. I think it deserves to add some discussions of this distinction in the supplementary materials, as it may be helpful for readers in the field.
2. In page 9, the authors argue that spin-singlet scenario cannot support the field-re-entrant superconductivity, by stating that “This is because the Zeeman effect of the magnetic field tends to suppress the spin-singlet superconducting state by inducing a depairing effect on spin singlet Cooper pairs,…”. I agree with this statement for the case of large magnetic field. However, in Fig.3b, the critical magnetic field B is only about 0.1 T, which may not induce strong depairing effect for spin-singlet pairing. Can d+id and d-id pairings account for observed two domains, given that they are time-reversal breaking and can couple with magnetic field?
3. The hysteresis and re-entrant superconductivity is explained by the formation of superconducting domains for varying magnetic field. The current heating and coupling measurements support this scenario for hysteresis (Fig.2h at 230 mK). I am curious whether similar measurements can be done at the temperature where re-entrant superconductivity appears, such as at 450 mK. This measurement will further strength the proposed scenario and conclusions of the paper.

### Reviewer 3

The authors have addressed the majority of my concerns and questions with their revisions, which have clarified their arguments for their interpretation of the data. While the results presented are not proof of p-wave superconductivity, they are certainly suggestive; the new title of the article is more appropriate to this level of evidence.
One minor correction from the first review seems to have been missed.
Original comment: The caption of Fig. S6 indicates that it is showing data for a variety of
magnetic field directions, presumably with the current direction fixed. However, the
text (lines 166-168) says, “In RbV3Sb5, the re-entrant superconductivity appears in all
current directions with respect to a fixed in-plane magnetic field direction (as shown in
Fig. S6 of Supplementary Information).” Which of these is accurate?
Response from authors: We apologize for the earlier misinformation and appreciate your attention to this detail. To clarify, we used a 3D vector magnet to rotate the in-plane magnetic field while keeping the current direction fixed. We have now corrected this in the manuscript.
Lines 188-190 in the new version still read, “in RbV3Sb5, the re-entrant superconductivity appears in all current directions with respect to a fixed in-plane magnetic field direction.”
Please correct this to indicate that the current direction is fixed and the magnetic field direction is changing.
In addition, please note the temperatures of measurements shown in Figs. S3, S4, S6, S8, S11, and S12 (either in figures themselves or in captions).
With the above changes, I would recommend the manuscript for publication.

### Reviewer 4

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

## Paper

## Abstract

The study of kagome materials has recently attracted much attention due to the presence of many electron-electron interaction-driven phases in a single material. In this work, we report the time-reversal symmetry-breaking superconductivity in the thin-flake kagome material RbV3Sb5. Firstly, when an in-plane magnetic field is swept in opposite directions, we observe an unconventional form of hysteresis in magnetoresistance, which is different from the hysteresis induced by extrinsic mechanisms. In contrast, no such hysteresis is observed in CsV3Sb5 samples below their superconducting transition temperature. Strikingly, at a fixed magnetic field, the finite-resistance state in RbV3Sb5 can be transitioned into the superconducting state by applying and subsequently removing a large current. Secondly, at temperatures around 400 mK, the re-entrance of superconductivity occurs during an in-plane field-sweeping process with a fixed sweeping direction. The observations of the unconventional hysteresis and re-entrance suggest the existence of time-reversal symmetry-breaking superconducting states in RbV3Sb5.

---

## Introduction

The discovery of kagome superconductors1–4 AV3Sb5 (A=K, Rb, Cs) has garnered significant attention in recent years due to the intriguing interplay of superconductivity5–14, charge density waves5,15–25, nematic orders20,23, pair density waves6,12,13, all within a single material. Such intricate interplay of the intertwined orders holds promise for uncovering unconventional phenomena, notably unconventional superconductivity5–14. Indeed, the nodal superconducting states have been observed in the kagome superconductor RbV3Sb5 with μSR experiments9, while nodeless superconductivity was suggested in the CsV3Sb5 compound26–29. Up to now, the mechanism of the superconducting properties of the AV3Sb5 family remains an open question4, necessitating further investigation and exploration.

Here, we report the unconventional superconductivity in the kagome material RbV3Sb5. The observed superconducting states in RbV3Sb5 are characterized by the emergence of the in-plane magnetic field-driven unconventional hysteresis in the resistance measurements, followed by the zero-field superconducting diode effect observed in an irradiated RbV3Sb5 sample that breaks inversion symmetry. In addition, by heating the sample with a large current and subsequently removing it, all at a fixed magnetic field within the hysteresis loop, the sample can be brought from a finite-resistance state to a superconducting state. Moreover, an asymmetric re-entrance of superconductivity driven by the in-plane magnetic field is observed at around 400 mK, showing two superconducting domes in the temperature-magnetic field phase diagram. Through magnetotransport experiments, we observe a distinct anisotropic two-fold symmetry of the in-plane upper critical fields in this centrosymmetric material. These findings underscore the unconventional and time-reversal symmetry breaking nature of superconductivity in RbV3Sb5.

---

## Results

Basicsuperconductingproperties
The kagome family AV3Sb5 represents a class of layered kagome superconductors, characterized by the alternating arrangement of V-Sb slabs, Sb slabs and A slabs. Specifically, RbV3Sb5 is a member of this family, which consists of V-Sb slabs interleaved with Rb layers. Each V-Sb slab exhibits a two-dimensional (2D) kagome net of V atoms, with Sb atoms occupying central positions of hexagons within the kagome lattice, as depicted in Fig. 1a. Evidently, this structural arrangement signifies a six-fold rotational symmetry. Figure 1b shows the calculated energy band of the kagome superconductor, highlighting an important feature near the Fermi energy: the parity mixing between the d-orbital of the V atom and the p-orbital of the Sb atom, introducing a spin-orbit-parity-coupling term30,31 in contrast to the conventional spin-orbit-coupling term. In the two-dimensional limit, this spin-orbit-parity-coupling term is responsible for the observation of the two-fold symmetric in-plane upper critical field in this centrosymmetric material30,31 which exhibits a nematic normal state20. In Fig. 1c, we present the current-voltage curves of the device at different temperatures, showcasing a characteristic superconducting behavior. Correspondingly, Fig. S1 shows the device image, in which the x-axis is roughly along the source-drain direction and the long axis of the sample. Figure 1d depicts the typical in-plane magnetic field dependence of the differential resistance dV/dI at a temperature T = 150 mK. Apparently, the critical current decreases with the magnetic field increasing, a hallmark of superconducting behavior. The in-plane superconducting coherence length is estimated to be around 137 nm according to the linearized Ginzburg–Landau (GL) expression32 Bc⊥ = Φ0 / 2πξ0^2(1 − T/Tc), where Φ0 is the magnetic flux quantum, ξ0 is the zero-temperature in-plane coherence length, and Tc is the critical temperature, as shown in Fig. S2.

Unconventional hysteretic superconducting behavior
We proceed by investigating the magnetic field dependence of the kagome superconductor RbV3Sb5. The configuration of the device is depicted in Fig. 2a. We employ a three-dimensional (3D) vector magnetic field to study the magnetic response of the superconducting states. In Fig. 2a, the direction of the magnetic field is defined by the θ and ϕ which are the polar angle and the azimuthal angle, respectively. Specifically, θ = ϕ = 0° denotes the direction of the x-axis. Remarkably, the magnetoresistance curve exhibits pronounced hysteretic behavior, as illustrated in Fig. 2b. When an in-plane magnetic field oriented along the x-direction is swept from −1 T to 1 T (red curve), the superconducting state is initially established at around −410 mT; then as the magnetic field turns positive, the resistance deviates from zero at about 210 mT, exhibiting pronounced asymmetry. Moreover, sweeping the field from 1 T back to −1 T (black curve), produces a mirrored response, thus uncovering hysteretic behavior. If we define the critical magnetic field by the magnitude of the magnetic field at which the resistance reaches 50% of the normal state resistance, then we get the critical values at the positive magnetic field during forward (denoted as B→) and backward (B←) sweeps as B→ = 380 mT and B← = 620 mT, respectively. Similar hysteresis is also observed when the magnetic field is applied along the y-axis as depicted in Fig. 2c. Figure 2e, f further show the hysteretic behavior observed during the field sweeping from 0 T to −1 T or 1 T, respectively. Notably, the critical field in the forward sweep is smaller than that in the backward sweep (B→ < B←), in sharp contrast to the trivial magnetic hysteresis (B→ > B←) typically observed in conventional superconductors33,34. This unusual behavior, as will be discussed later, points to broken time-reversal symmetry in the superconducting state. Additional evidence for such symmetry breaking is provided by the zero-field superconducting diode effect observed in the irradiated RbV3Sb5 sample that breaks inversion symmetry (Fig. S3).

An atural question is whether such hysteretic behavior is exclusively confined to the in-plane orientation. To answer this question, we conduct the out-of-plane magnetic field angle dependence of the hysteresis. As depicted in Fig. 2g, our findings demonstrate that at an out-of-plane angle θ = ±9°, the hysteresis is destroyed. Such out-of-plane magnetic field angle dependence suggests that the hysteresis is related to the in-plane magnetization of the superconducting state. Consequently, this rules out the possibility that the hysteresis is triggered by the out-of-plane component of the magnetic field.

The two-fold symmetric upper critical field
We further study the ϕ-dependence of the magnetoresistance under the in-plane magnetic field. The magnetoresistance as a function of ϕ are shown in Fig. 2d. A distinct two-fold symmetric behavior is evident. The extraction of the upper critical fields is further illustrated in Fig. S4a. As shown in the theoretical calculations (Fig. S4b) within the single-layer limit, the presence of the nematic order and the spin-orbit-parity-coupling (SOPC)30,31 can lead to a two-fold symmetric upper critical field (details can be found in the Supplementary Information) even when the orbital effects of the in-plane magnetic field are ignored. Due to the finite thickness of the sample, the orbital effects of the magnetic field can also induce this two-fold symmetry35,36, given the six-fold rotational symmetry is broken by the nematic order in the normal state20. The extra contribution of the orbital effect only changes the results quantitatively. The key conclusion of observed two-fold symmetric upper critical field is that the original D6h point group symmetry is reduced to D2h due to the presence of the nematic state.

The current heating and cooling experiment
In Fig. 2h, the result of the current heating and cooling experiment is depicted. Initially, as the magnetic field sweeps from −1 T to 270 mT (illustrated by the red curve) and the system enters into the state with non-zero resistance. At this point, we apply a large current to heat up the sample to suppress superconductivity completely. Subsequently, removing the current allows the system to cool down and enter into the superconducting state, as indicated by the red curve. Notably, with further increasing the magnetic field to 1 T, the resistance curve closely resembles the one observed during the magnetic field’s reversal from 1 T to 270 mT (shown by black curve). Furthermore, by repeating the current heating and cooling experiment while sweeping the magnetic field from 1 T to −270 mT (black curve), a similar phenomenon is observed. This finding clearly shows that the finite-resistance state within the hysteresis loop is a metastable state which has a higher energy than the ground state. As will be discussed below, this observation provides crucial evidence for the existence of superconducting domains in the sample.

Magnetic field driven re-entrance of superconductivity
Subsequently, an investigation into the temperature dependence of the magnetoresistance is studied. As temperature rises, superconductivity can be suppressed by thermal effects. Figure 3a, b show the temperature-magnetic field phase diagram and waterfall plot of the temperature dependence of the magnetoresistance curve, respectively, while the complete temperature-magnetic field phase diagram is available in the supplementary Fig. S6a. Remarkably, within Fig. 3a, two distinct superconducting domes are observed in the magnetoresistance measurements when the magnetic field changes from −1 T to 1 T. Initially, the superconductivity is destroyed at a finite magnetic field of 80 mT at 400 mK. However, a second dome of superconductivity is observed when the magnetic field becomes larger in the positive direction. Such a phenomenon of re-entrant superconductivity persists across a temperature span from 400 mK to 600 mK. When the sweep direction of the magnetic field is reversed, the corresponding mapping figure will be mirrored, as shown in Fig. S6b. Furthermore, the re-entrant superconducting states are also observed for magnetic fields in all in-plane directions, corroborated in the supplementary Fig. S7. We label these two distinct superconducting phases as “SC-I” (the superconducting dome obtained before the re-entrance of superconductivity) and “SC-II” (the superconducting dome obtained after the re-entrance of superconductivity) as shown in Fig. 3a. The temperature dependence of the re-entrant behavior is shown in Fig. 3b.

Figure 3c shows the θ-dependence of the magnetoresistance. It is shown that superconductivity in SC-II is eliminated when the out-of-plane magnetic field angle exceeds 6° while SC-I still exists. This observation underscores the greater fragility of SC-II to out-of-plane magnetic field components. To further display the two superconducting domes SC-I and SC-II of the material, we measured dV/dI as a function of the magnetic field and applied current at different temperatures37 as shown in Fig. 3d. Two superconducting domes SC-I and SC-II are clearly observed. Similar hysteresis and re-entrant behavior are reproduced and Figs. S8, 9 show the results for samples #2 and #3.

Ruling out trivial origins
Although hysteresis in magnetoresistance can be induced by superheating and supercooling effects33,34 or the flux-trapping effects38–40 as shown in previous works, the hysteresis loops observed in Fig. 2 are distinct from the hysteresis observed in previous experiments.

In the hysteresis induced by the superheating-supercooling effect, sweeping the magnetic field from 0 T to 1 T (forward sweep) and then gradually reducing the magnetic field from 1 T back to 0 T (backward sweep) must result in a higher upper critical field during the forward sweep compared to the backward sweep33. In contrast, our observations, as illustrated in Fig. 2f, reveal that during the forward sweep from 0 T to 1 T (indicated by the blue curve), the upper critical field B0 is smaller than the upper critical field B← in the backward sweep (indicated by the black curve). The same result is obtained when the magnetic field is swept from 0 T to −1 T and then reduced gradually, as shown in Fig. 2e by the blue and red curves. Such findings exclude the superheating and supercooling mechanism caused by the magnetic field induced local minima of the free energy of the superconductor41.

In addition, the hysteresis observed in our experiment exhibits behavior starkly distinct from that attributed to the flux-trapping mechanism. In the hysteresis induced by the flux-trapping, a magnetoresistance minimum at finite magnetic field can be observed in the backward-sweeping curve (returning curve)40,42,43. In contrast, as shown in Fig. 2b, c and Fig. S10 in Supplementary Information, in RbV3Sb5, no magnetoresistance minimum at finite field was observed in the backward-sweeping curve over a wider range of applied currents. Moreover, we conducted in-plane field-sweep experiments on over ten thin-flake kagome material CsV3Sb5. Although RbV3Sb5 and CsV3Sb5 belong to the same kagome material family and the thin flakes we used have similar thicknesses, no such hysteresis was observed in CsV3Sb5 below its superconducting transition temperature, as shown in Fig. S11. If the observed hysteresis were due to trivial mechanisms, such as flux trapping, rather than intrinsic properties of the superconducting states, it should also appear in CsV3Sb5 as well. This result suggests that the superconducting states of RbV3Sb5 and CsV3Sb5 are different, and the hysteresis originates from the intrinsic superconducting properties of RbV3Sb5. It is interesting to note that Knight shift experiments in CsV3Sb5 suggested spin singlet pairing44. However, since our control experiments suggest that the superconducting properties of RbV3Sb5 are quite different from CsV3Sb5, the pairing symmetry of RbV3Sb5 is possibly unconventional.

Furthermore, the re-entrant superconductivity observed in our experiments is different from the re-entrance observed in conventional superconductors45–47 which relies on vortex pinning induced by applied magnetic field. In contrast to some trivial re-entrant superconductivity observed only in specific directions, i.e. current parallel to magnetic field46, in RbV3Sb5, the re-entrant superconductivity appears in all in-plane magnetic field directions with respect to a fixed current direction (as shown in Fig. S7 of Supplementary Information). What’s more, the trivial reentrance induced by vortex pinning can only give rise to asymmetric B-T phase diagram45,47. This contradicts the asymmetric B-T phase diagram observed experimentally as shown in Fig. 3a. Therefore, the simultaneous observation of both in-plane magnetic field hysteresis and asymmetric re-entrant superconductivity rules out trivial origins, indicating the need for a novel explanation.

Possible pairing symmetries
Considering the key observations in experiments reported above, we discuss the possible pairing symmetries in the kagome superconductor RbV3Sb5. First of all, the observed novel hysteresis in magnetoresistance measurements suggests spontaneous breaking of time-reversal symmetry, which is further corroborated by the zero-field superconducting diode effect observed in an irradiated RbV3Sb5 sample that breaks inversion symmetry (see Fig. S3 in the Supplementary Information for details). It is noted that the time-reversal symmetry may be broken in the normal states of the kagome family AV3Sb5 due to loop currents in the charge density wave phase15,16,22,23. However, the loop currents would produce out-of-plane magnetization, in contrast to the in-plane magnetic moments observed in this work. Therefore, the in-plane hysteresis is likely caused by the superconducting state itself, rather than the normal state. Moreover, as shown in Fig. 2g, the magnetoresistance hysteresis is weakened by the out-of-plane component of the magnetic field. The reason is as follows: RbV3Sb5 is a quasi-two-dimensional superconductor48, where the out-of-plane resistivity is approximately 33 times greater than the in-plane resistivity at low temperatures. In such materials, an out-of-plane magnetic field rapidly suppresses superconductivity due to the orbital effects, which generates many vortices within the superconducting plane. When the applied magnetic field has a sizable out-of-plane component, many vortices will be created, and the vortices will dominate the transport properties of the superconducting films. As the transport is mostly dominated by vortices, the magnetoresistance behaves in a similar way for both the up-sweep and down-sweep fields, leading to the disappearance of hysteresis. A similar behavior is also observed in the heavy-fermion superconductor UCoGe49, where a slight tilt of the magnetic field toward the c-axis leads to a significant decrease in the upper critical field and the disappearance of hysteresis.

In addition to the pronounced hysteresis, the observation of re-entrant superconductivity as the magnetic field increases suggests that the SC-II phase can be stabilized by the magnetic field. After carefully ruling out trivial origins, the spin-singlet scenario cannot support the field-induced re-entrant superconductivity. This is because the Zeeman effect of the magnetic field tends to suppress the spin-singlet superconducting state by inducing a depairing effect on spin-singlet Cooper pairs, whereas it does not affect the equal-spin pairing states. Therefore, the reappearance of the superconducting state under a larger magnetic field is not consistent with the spin-singlet Cooper pairs scenario. Instead, the observed re-entrance is more consistent with equal-spin pairing, where the spin-magnetic moments of the Cooper pairs couple to the magnetic field, lowering the energy of the superconducting state. Moreover, within the hysteresis loop, the transition of the finite resistance state to the superconducting state upon applying and then removing the current indicates that the finite resistance state is a metastable state. This suggests that there can be different superconducting domains with opposite spin polarizations in the finite resistance state, similar to the case of a ferromagnet with magnetic domains. Furthermore, due to the centrosymmetric point group symmetry, the superconducting pairing should be odd parity due to the spin-triplet pairing50. Therefore, the orbital part of the pairing should be p-wave or f-wave in nature51–64. These large number of novel properties observed in the superconducting state place strong constraints on the pairing symmetry of RbV3Sb5.

Since the superconducting pairing is formed near the Fermi surface, we project the four-orbital (eight-band) model into the manifestly covariant pseudospin basis (MCPB)30,65,66 by choosing two degenerate bands (jk, αi, jk, αi) near the Fermi surface as the projecting targets. Here, k is the crystal momentum and α is the pseudo-spin index (The detail can be found in the Method Section and the Supplementary Information). It is important to note that the original point group symmetry of the material is D6h. Before the superconducting transition happens, the nematic order parameter comes in references20,23 and reduces the point group symmetry to D2h. Therefore, the superconducting order parameters can be constructed by using basis functions belonging to irreducible representations of the point group D2h. As mentioned above, this pairing state must possess net in-plane spin polarization. The possible superconducting order parameters represented by the d-vectors are listed in Table 1. Importantly, both of these are nodal topological p-wave, spin-triplet, time-reversal-symmetry-breaking states. As shown in the Supplementary Information, both of these states possess Majorana flat bands at the sample boundaries. In the following, we choose the B3u representation without loss of generality.

The matrix representation of the superconducting gap in the MCPB is Δ = (d·σ)iσ2, where the σi (i=1,2,3) are the Pauli matrices. The nodes of these two order parameters belonging to different representations are located on x-axis and y-axis, respectively. The parameter ξ controls the amplitude of the spin polarization: 1−η = 1−|cos(2ξ)2 + sin(2ξ)2|, which is determined by the specific form of the interactions in this material, while the parameter χ controls the spin-polarization direction of the Cooper pairs. The orientation of the spin polarization p of the Cooper pair is given by: p = id×d*/(sin(χ), −cos(χ), 0), which is coupled with the effective magnetic field gk in the MCPB in the form of −gk·p. Therefore, the direction of the spin polarization can be pinned by the applied magnetic field (See Supplementary Information for detail). When the magnetic field changes its sign, superconducting domains with opposite spin-polarization become energetically favorable and can be created.

A possible mechanism for the hysteresis, current heating and cooling experiments, and re-entrant superconductivity
Here, we provide a possible, schematic superconducting domain picture to explain the hysteresis in resistance, the current heating and cooling experiments as well as the reentrant superconductivity observed in RbV3Sb5. As discussed in last section, the system has spin-polarized triplet pairing components which can form the superconducting domains67,68 where Cooper pairs with net spin-polarization act like miniature magnets with different polarization directions, similar to ferromagnetic domains. At a low temperature for example (as denoted by T1 in Fig. 4), when the magnetic field sweeps from −1 T to 1 T, the system initially enters into a superconducting state dominated by negative domains. The negative domains are formed by spin-polarized Cooper pairs with magnetic moments pointing to the negative direction as indicated by blue arrows in Fig. 4. In other words, the spin-polarized Cooper pairs can form domains and the external magnetic field aligns the magnetization direction of the domains. When the magnetic field changes sign, superconducting domains with positive magnetization direction (positive domains) emerge. As the magnetic field further increases in the positive direction, positive domains become dominant, but the negative domains can still coexist. Therefore, at a positive magnetic field, we expect that the system enters into a metastable state characterized by the coexistence of the positive and negative domains as shown in Fig. 4. On the other hand, if the magnetic field is swept from 1 T to the same positive magnetic field, the domains are dominantly positive and the superconducting state will have a lower free energy. This provides a possible explanation for the hysteretic behavior of the resistance. Moreover, at a fixed positive magnetic field ~0.27 T (Fig. 2h), we can use a large current to heat the metastable finite-resistance state with both positive and negative domains and then remove the current under a fixed magnetic field, the system can transition to the superconducting ground state, where superconducting domains predominantly align with the applied magnetic field. This current heating and cooling experiment strongly supports the superconducting domain picture of our theory which suggests that the SC-II state is a metastable state containing superconducting domains with different spin polarizations. In addition, in Fig. S13, three curves of distinct colors correspond to different initial magnetic fields (1 T for the black curve, 0 T for the blue curve, and −1 T for the red curve) at the onset of the field sweeping. These disparate trajectories, as illustrated in Fig. S13, indicate that the magnetic response of the superconducting state in RbV3Sb5 is determined by the initial magnetic field, thereby further supporting the domain picture.

At a higher temperature (as denoted by T2 in Fig. 4), when the magnetic field sweeps from −1 T to 1 T, the system is initially in a superconducting state with negative domains. When the magnetic field changes sign from negative to positive, the negative domains shrink and the positive domains start to form as in the low temperature cases. However, due to the thermal effect, these domains are too small to be connected spatially to form a superconducting state. As the magnetic field increases, the positive domains become more energetically favorable to form. The enlargement of positive domains allows percolation of superconducting domains to give rise to superconducting state. This percolation picture gives a mechanism for the re-entrance of superconductivity at around 400 mK as observed in the experiment. Therefore, the nodal p-wave superconductivity belonging to the B2u or the B3u representation of the D2h point group, which enables Cooper pairs exhibiting net spin-polarization, can provide a reasonable explanation of all the observed novel phenomena in RbV3Sb5.

In summary, we report experimental evidence for time-reversal-symmetry-breaking superconductivity in RbV3Sb5. This conclusion is supported by several experimental observations. First, we observed a magnetoresistance hysteresis in the superconducting state. Importantly, the superconducting diode effect in inversion-symmetry-broken samples at zero field clearly demonstrated the time-reversal symmetry breaking properties of the superconducting state. Furthermore, the magnetic hysteresis is absent in our CsV3Sb5 samples, which suggests distinct superconducting mechanisms in the two systems, despite both belonging to the same kagome family. Our work suggests RbV3Sb5 is a new platform for realizing unconventional and time-reversal symmetry breaking superconductivity.

## Methods

Sample fabrication
The thin films of RbV3Sb5 were exfoliated using polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) from the bulk crystal onto silicon substrates with a 285 nm oxide layer. The fabrication of pre-patterned metal electrodes was achieved using the standard electron-beam lithography (EBL) method, followed by deposition of a Ti/Au (10 nm/50 nm) through electron-beam evaporation. Then, the device was encapsulated with hBN to prevent any degradation due to air atmosphere. All device fabrication procedures mentioned above were performed in a controlled environment within a nitrogen-filled glovebox with oxygen and water levels below 0.01 ppm to minimize any potential degradation of the samples.

Quantum transport measurements
The samples were measured in an Oxford dilution refrigerator Triton XL1000 equipped with a vector magnet. This setup allowed the samples to remain stationary while a real three-dimensional vector magnetic field was applied. Such a technique greatly improves the precision of the magnetic field angle-deviation measurements, effectively circumventing the issues of return differences and heat generation commonly associated with mechanical rotators.

The dV/dI measurements were conducted with a rather small alternative current (i.e., 100 nA or 10 nA) while applying a much larger direct current (i.e., 10 μA). To optimize the signal-to-noise ratio in these experiments, a standard lock-in technique was employed, along with the implementation of essential low-temperature filters.

Conducting the strict in-plane magnetic field measurements with the 3D vector magnet
1. Initially, we securely mounted the sample within the dilution refrigerator. Despite our meticulous efforts to align the sample with the magnetic field axis, a minor discrepancy persisted.
2. In response to this, our subsequent step involved the calibration of the vector magnetic field. What sets our approach apart from the traditional mechanical rotational system is that we did not need to physically rotate the sample plane, we could fine-tune the value of the vector magnetic field, which would greatly enhance the angle accuracy.
3. During the calibration process, we initially conducted angle-dependent measurements of the critical magnetic field of the sample in both the XZ and YZ planes. Given that our sample plane was mounted in the XY plane, these measurements allowed us to determine the angle deviation from the sample plane. With the calibration of the XZ-plane and YZ-plane, then the new coordinates are achieved, with strict alignment of the vector magnetic field within the XY plane. It’s worth noting that our device substrate consisted of a rigid silicon wafer with a 285 nm SiO2 layer. Through this dual-axis calibration process, we can confidently assert that the calibrated XY plane remains strictly within the sample plane, with an error margin of less than 0.1°.

Ruling out trivial origins of two-fold symmetric superconductivity
It has been suggested that the anisotropy may arise from current-induced vortex motion. Such a scenario was ruled out by different configurations in our previous paper69. The two-fold symmetric axis is independent on the current direction. Specifically speaking, in both cases that the current is applied in-plane with ϕ=90° and ϕ=0°, the in-plane azimuthal angular dependence of the magnetoresistance exhibited the same twofold symmetry pattern, irrespective of the current direction. Thus, the two-fold symmetry is independent of the current direction, ruling out the possible vortex origin.

Manifestly covariant pseudospin basis (MCPB)
Due to the existence of the inversion symmetry, though there is SOPC30,31, one can always define a pseudospin basis, in which the orbital and pseudospin degrees of freedom are decoupled. On the other hand, since the superconducting pairing happens near the Fermi surface, we can project the four-orbital (eight-band) model into a two degenerate band basis with different pseudospins, which is named as the manifestly covariant pseudospin basis (MCPB)30,65,66. In this basis, the magnetic field couples to the spin in this form:
Hz = μB Σk,α,β,i,j c†kα aij(k)σij βckβ, (1)
where μB means the Bohr magnetron, α, β label the pseudospin of the fermion in band basis, σi (i=1,2,3) are Pauli metrices. Here, aij(k) (i,j=1,2,3) come from the projection to MCPB (See Supplementary Information for detail), which change the original magnetic field Bi into a k-dependent effective magnetic field gk = μB a(k)B. Including the pairing order parameter, the total Hamiltonian of the superconducting state can be written as:
Htotal = Σk,α εk c†kα ckα + Σk,αβ [ (d·σ)iσ2 ] αβ c†kα c†−kβ + h.c. + Hz, (2)
where the d-vector is the possible order parameter of the odd-parity superconductivity which is show in Table 1. With the total Hamiltonian Htotal, one can calculate the topological properties and the magnetic responses conveniently. Importantly, this Hamiltonian describes a nodal topological p-wave superconductor which possesses the Majorana flat bands70–77 on the edges of the samples78–82 (See Fig. S13 in Supplementary Information for the result of the open boundary calculations).

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In their manuscript entitled "Spin-polarized p-wave superconductivity in the kagome material RbV3Sb5", Shuo Wang et al. measure magnetotransport in devices of RbV3Sb5. They have three main observations: 1) hysteresis of the resistance in field; 2) field-reentrant superconductivity that is asymmetric in field direction; and 3) two-fold anisotropy in the in-plane critical field. They use these observations to motivate the presence of a chiral p-wave superconducting state.
Possible chiral p-wave superconductors have a long and messy history, and thus these strong claims require equally strong evidence. Unfortunately, Wang et al. do not appear to provide it. My main concerns are:
1) Hysteresis in superconductors usually arises due to vortex physics. Their argument against this is based on their quenching scheme, whereby they apply a large current to drive the sample normal, then cool it in a finite field. This resets the flux trapping state based on whatever field they cool in. They claim flux will be trapped at weak pinning sites that should be mobile enough be dissipative. I don’t know how they can make that claim. This depends entirely on the microscopics of the the pinning site strength, the amount of current, the energy barrier at the edge of the sample for vortices, etc, none of which are known. Also, the authors state that "In the positive magnetic field region, we obtain a newly formed superconducting state with zero resistance", but see point 3 below where I point out that zero resistance is never seen.
-1b) Did the authors check how the hysteresis depends on the applied current? Do the authors get same hysteretic behavior with more or less current?
2) The authors claim that the superconducting state breaks the C6 rotation symmetry of the lattice down to C2. However, this symmetry is already broken by the CDW at higher temperatures! See e.g. https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1674-1056/acd8b1/pdf Once a symmetry is reduced, all measured quantities in general have that lower symmetry, e.g. the critical field is expected to be C2 symmetric in the CDW state even if it is a trivial s-wave state.
-2b) There may be domains of the CDW that produce a higher effective symmetry at long length scales. However, this is a mesoscopic device with a very high aspect ratio that will naturally favor one domain of the others. This has the prediction that the anisotropy in the critical field could be device dependent, and indeed a subset of the present authors published exactly this data in an earlier paper https://www.nature.com/articles/s42005-023-01496-3#Sec10 that shows a MUCH higher anisotropy than the data in the current paper. Why should the anisotropy be device dependent if it was intrinsic to the superconducting state?
3) The authors claim re-entrant superconductivity. However, the authors never measure a zero-resistance state at ANY field or temperature - there is always a substantial offset. Why is this the case? The reentrance only goes close to the zero-field resistance (which again, is not zero resistance) in a very, very narrow temperature range around 400 mK, otherwise it is just a dip in resistance.
-3b) Very similar measurements were performed on the same material in an earlier paper by a subset of the current authors https://www.nature.com/articles/s42005-023-01496-3#Sec10 why was no reentrant superconductivity observed in this device?
4) The absolute highest the upper critical field could be is 0.75 tesla for field in plane (taken as the field where the resistance becomes flat in Fig 2b). This is very close to the Pauli limit of ~1 tesla (calculated using a g-factor of 2). If RbV3Sb5 is spin triplet, why is the upper critical field Pauli limited for field in the plane?

### Reviewer 2

The authors present intriguing magnetotransport findings in kagome superconductor RbV3Sb5 thin films, including hysteresis in magnetoresistance, reentrance of superconductivity, and a two-fold symmetric in-plane upper critical field. By conducting additional measurements, they ruled out trivial explanations for these phenomena. The authors propose that spin-polarized p-wave pairing could account for the observed results. Currently, the pairing symmetry of kagome superconductors is still under debate from both experimental and theoretical perspective. The present results are interesting and offer more insights into the pairing state of thin-film kagome superconductors. However, it is important to note that this evidence presented is not definitive proof of p-wave pairing, particularly given knight shift measurements suggesting spin-singlet pairing in the bulk (Chin. Phys. Lett. 38 077402 (2021)).
I suggest that the authors should temper their assertion of p-wave pairing in the manuscript and explicitly acknowledge the indirect nature of the evidence provided. Nevertheless, the paper offers valuable experimental insights and features a well-executed theoretical analysis. The authors should properly address the following concerns before my recommendation of publication:
1. The authors discuss the band dispersion with the spin-orbit-parity-coupling term and its relevance to the two-fold in-plane upper critical field. However, according to fig.4a in PRL 125, 247002 (2020), the SOC gap between p- and d-orbital band along Gamma-M (located at 0.5 eV) is far away from the Fermi level. Why is such term relevant for the band dispersion and properties of kagome superconductor AV3Sb5?
2. Clarification is needed regarding the measuring temperature in Fig.2h. Additionally, if a quenching process is involved in the measurement shown in Fig.3b, it is essential to determine if a similar zero resistance can be achieved for a positive magnetic field. If this is the case, can this be called re-entrant superconductivity by sweeping magnetic field (as superconductivity is not destroyed)? Conventionally, re-entrant superconductivity is characterized by the reappearance of superconductivity as the magnetic field increases after being suppressed by a magnetic field.
3. How might the temperature-magnetic field phase diagram in Fig.2 be altered by conducting measurements with a fixed magnetic field and varying temperature?
4. The bulk superconductivity (CsV3Sb5) is spin-singlet according to Chin. Phys. Lett. 38 077402 (2021). In contrast, the authors claim a spin-triplet pairing in RbV3Sb5 thin films, with a transition temperature close to that of the bulk material. It is difficult to understand why there will be a transition from spin-singlet to spin-triplet pairing between bulk and thin films. The author should provide more discussions about the difference between bulk and thin films. The relatively low upper critical field observed in the thin films challenges the expectation for a spin-triplet pairing. Will a time-reversal symmetry breaking spin-singlet pairing explain some of experimental phenomena? If not, possible mechanism of spin-triplet pairing in thin films should be further discussed.

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, the authors present magnetoresistance measurements of the kagome material RbV3Sb5 in order to investigate the nature of its superconducting state. One of their most notable findings is the hysteresis in magnetoresistance —namely in the boundaries of the superconducting state—for magnetic fields swept in opposite directions. The authors have measured this hysteresis for a variety of field directions and temperatures.
The authors have demonstrated that this hysteresis is present for all directions of in-plane fields, yet disappears with a small tilt of field outside the ab plane. They also show that there is a range of temperatures, roughly 400-600 mK, for which the superconductivity is split into two domes as a function of field, with a higher-resistance state appearing at roughly 80 mT for forwards field sweeps and -80 mT for backwards field sweeps between the two domes.
In addition, with the sample in a finite field, the authors have used applied current to heat their sample into the normal state and then removed the current and allowed it to cool. They have showed that this process can bring the sample from a finite-resistance state to a zero-resistance state. This supports the authors’ hypothesis that the finite-resistance state in the hysteresis loop is related to domain formation, rather than being due to flux trapping. They posit that this is due to time-reversal symmetry-breaking superconducting order that can couple to applied magnetic fields.
The hysteretic behavior presented here is novel and interesting. The authors have studied this behavior thoroughly in terms of field direction and temperature. Their use of current heating/cooling to further understand the finite-resistance state is excellent. The authors also put forward a sensible model by which to interpret their data, which indicates that the material is a topological superconductor, certainly of interest to the field.
However, there are a few points that I would like to see addressed:
•The authors note that “the AV3Sb5 family lacks magnetic orders in the normal state”, and thus attribute the time-reversal symmetry-breaking to the superconducting phase itself. However, as pointed out in the authors’ Ref. 4, the charge density wave orders of this family of materials do appear to break time-reversal symmetry. The authors should discuss whether time-reversal symmetry-breaking from the CDW of RbV3Sb5 could be the cause of the observed hysteresis.
•The authors indicate that the superconductivity is spin-triplet based on the observed time-reversal symmetry-breaking. However, it is possible for spin-singlet superconductors to break time-reversal symmetry; see, e.g., Phys. Rev. B 105, 155101 (2022). If the authors have experimental or theoretical reasons to support this superconducting phase being spin-triplet, they should make those arguments explicitly.
•In the explanation of their proposed mechanism, the authors do not address the effect of out-of-plane magnetic fields as seen in their measurements. In the model involving superconducting domains, why should an out-of-plane field component destroy hysteresis?
•It would be useful to see data showing if there are any memory effects. For example, if the sample goes from -1 T to 1 T, back to -1 T and again to 1 T, does the initial forwards sweep look the same as the second forward sweep?
•Given the difference in critical fields for different field directions, it is interesting to note that the split between SC-I and SC-II seems to occur at the same magnetic field value regardless of the magnetic field direction, if I am interpreting Fig. S6 correctly. I am curious if the authors have any comment on this behavior.
•The similarity between the hysteresis seen in this compound and that observed in UCoGe is interesting; see Appl. Phys. Lett. 98, 132507 (2011). The hysteresis in UCoGe has the same qualitative behavior and also disappears for fields tilted slightly out of plane. I believe this similarity merits at least a mention, if not discussion.
In addition, certain points in the text could benefit from clarification:
•In the abstract:
“Strikingly, at a fixed magnetic field, the finite-resistance state can be quenched to the zero-resistance state by applying a large current.”
If I understand correctly, the statement should be: “…by applying and subsequently removing a large current.” It also might be worth noting here that the purpose of the current is sample heating.
•Lines 13-15:
“In addition, at a fixed magnetic field, a large current can suppress superconductivity completely at the finite-resistance state by heating. Incredibly, upon the removal of the current and cooling, the sample can be quenched to a zero-resistance state.”
I understand why the authors refer to superconductivity in the finite-resistance state, having read the full article. For the sake of introducing the subject to new readers, I suggest something like the following:
“In addition, by heating the sample with a large current and subsequently cooling it, all at a fixed magnetic field within the hysteresis loop, the sample can be brought from a finite-resistance state to a zero-resistance state.”
•Lines 35-36:
“Each V-Sb slab exhibits a two-dimensional (2D) kagome net of V atoms, forming a hexagonal structure with Sb atoms occupying central positions…”
I believe it would be more accurate to say,
“Each V-Sb slab exhibits a two-dimensional (2D) kagome net of V atoms, with Sb atoms occupying central positions of the hexagons within the kagome lattice…”
•Throughout the text, “quench” is used to refer to the heating of the sample above the superconducting temperature as well as the cooling of the sample. This terminology is somewhat confusing, as “quench” can be used to refer to superconducting magnets unintentionally becoming normal, or to a quick-cooling process. It may be more clear to refer simply to heating and cooling via current.
•Were all sweeps starting at a finite magnetic field actually cooled in that field, as opposed to zero-field-cooled? If so, was in-field cooling always done from room temperature, or from some other temperature?
•In the section “A proposed mechanism…”, when discussing the current heating/cooling experiment, the authors could be more explicit that in their model, cooling under an applied field results in superconducting domains that are predominantly aligned with the field, thus leading to a zero-resistance state.
•In Fig. S3a, “lower critical field” is used. I believe the authors are referring to the critical field that is at a lower value due to hysteresis. However, given that “lower critical field” already has a defined meaning for superconductors, a different term should be used (perhaps “greater” and “lesser” critical fields?) and the caption should clarify what is meant by these.
•The caption of Fig. S6 indicates that it is showing data for a variety of magnetic field directions, presumably with the current direction fixed. However, the text (lines 166-168) says, “In RbV3Sb5, the re-entrant superconductivity appears in all current directions with respect to a fixed in-plane magnetic field direction (as shown in Fig. S6 of Supplementary Information).” Which of these is accurate?
•Additionally, at what temperature were the data for Fig. S6 taken? This should be indicated in the figure caption.
•Similarly, at what temperature were the data for Fig. 3c taken? This should be indicated in the figure caption.
•Is the normal-state resistance of the sample actually 1 Ohm, as shown in Fig. 1d, or is this a normalization?
•The authors cite Ref. 22 on line 143 when discussing the superheating-supercooling effect. However, I do not believe that Ref. 22 touches on superheating/supercooling. Is this the correct reference?
The following changes are also suggested to improve figure legibility:
•Adding tick marks along the axes for all figures that don’t have them:
2d, 3a, 3c, S4, S5a&b, S6a
•Possibly adding arrows and/or labels to Fig. 2h along the “quenching” segments, to indicate the heating and subsequent cooling

The ratio of the normal-state resistance to residual resistance of superconducting states in our samples ranges from 10 to 100, depending on the micro-fabrication quality. This variability is an inherent challenge in thin-film fabrication and measurements. Unlike bulk superconductors, thin films are quasi-2D systems that are particularly susceptible to quasiparticles, thermal fluctuations, and fabrication defects. Specifically, RbV Sb has a T of only ~ 900 mK. Even at 3 5 c temperatures as low as 100 mK (well below T ), thermal fluctuations can induce c phase decoherence between different superconducting regions which can cause dissipations. In comparison, thin-flake CsV Sb , with a higher T 2.5 - 3.8 K, 3 5 c exhibits residual resistance more than an order of magnitude smaller than that of RbV Sb , as confirmed by our experiments. 3 5 ii. While bulk AV Sb samples are relatively stable, 3 5 their exfoliated thin flakes are highly sensitive to environmental factors, such as oxygen exposure. Response: We thank the referee for pointing out this important issue. Indeed, re-entrant superconductivity is not observed in all samples. Statistically, over 50% of our samples exhibit such re-entrant superconductivity. This is because the emergence of the second superconducting dome requires percolation of superconducting domains. When sweeping the magnetic field from negative to positive values, the magnetic field initially suppresses superconductivity after the first dome. Subsequently, the superconducting domains must grow and reconnect to form the second superconducting dome. In an ideal case, re-entrant superconductivity would be observed at an intermediate temperature. However, in practice, the reconnection of superconducting domains is highly sensitive to disorder and defects, which vary between devices, particularly in thin-flake samples. Thus, there is a possibility that the domains will fail to reconnect again and form the second superconducting dome. During the preparation of our previously published work, we also observed re-entrant superconductivity in several samples. However, at the time, we did not fully understand the underlying mechanism, and thus, the focus of that manuscript was primarily on the two-fold symmetric superconductivity. The current study represents significant progress in our understanding.
